newsitem.title: USA: Florida weighs new execution method after foul-up.
newsitem.headline: Florida weighs new execution method after foul-up.

text.p: Florida's attorney general asked lawmakers on Wednesday to consider replacing the state's notorious electric chair with lethal injection following a botched execution in which flames and smoke leapt from a condemned man's head as he died.

State Attorney General Bob Butterworth made the request in a letter to state House and Senate leaders a day after the 74-year-old electric chair malfunctioned during the execution of Cuban immigrant Pedro Medina.
Medina, who maintained his innocence to the end, was executed for the 1982 murder of an Orlando school teacher despite appeals for mercy on his behalf from Pope John Paul II and others.

During the execution, witnesses said a five to six-inch (12-16 cm) flame shot from the right side of Medina's head shortly after the state's executioner pulled the switch that sent 2000 volts of electricity surging through his body. The room filled with white, acrid smoke that witnesses said smelled of burned flesh and a prison official had to open a window.

An attending medical examiner said in a sworn statement that Medina died instantly, before the flames and smoke, but Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles ordered an independent autopsy and review of the state's execution procedures.

"Regardless of the outcome of that review, condemned murderers are certain to once again raise electrocution as an appellate issue as they seek to avoid their lawfully imposed sentences," Butterworth said in a letter to Senate President Toni Jennings and Speaker of the House Daniel Webster.
"This will serve to delay even further the justice due the families of the victims of their horrible crimes, justice that already is delayed much too long," he wrote.
Medina's execution was the second malfunction in seven years for the device, a three-legged oak chair built by prison inmates and first used in 1924.

In 1990, a synthetic sponge used to replace an old natural sponge in the helmet worn during the execution of Jesse Tafero caught fire as the current passed through it, and the current had to be turned off and on three times to keep the headpiece from exploding into flame. Tafero's body drew spasmodic breaths in response to the current while ashes fell to his shoulders.
That incident brought Florida's capital punishment system to a standstill while appeals were filed over the chair's use.
